t: "I thank God" or just "I give thanks"
p: The Byzantine text names God as the one thanked.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
NA28, Tregelles, Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV)

why: This entry names only the editions. The SBL, Tyndale House and Westcott-Hort texts omit "to God"; NA28, Tregelles, the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus have it. The longer wording is the usual opening of such sentences in Paul (1:4), so a scribe could easily have added it. The meaning is the same.

p: The oldest text and the Byzantine text differ by one letter-group.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine majority text, Textus Receptus (KJV: "I had baptized")

why: "You were baptized into my name" is the reading of NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles. "I baptized in my own name" looks like a smoothing: it repeats the verb of 1:14. The first reading also gives the stronger line: the Corinthians were baptized into Christ, not into Paul. The two readings differ little in sense.
b: The KJV follows the second reading: "Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name." The Greek is a single word either way.

p: The Byzantine text adds "this".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV)

why: The shorter reading has the wide support of the editions, and the longer matches 3:19 ("the wisdom of this world"), which suggests a scribe added the word to match.

p: A one-letter difference changes plural to singular.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV)

why: The plural has the support of the editions and fits Jewish requests for repeated proofs (Mark 8:11; John 4:48). The singular could echo Matthew 12:38.

p: The KJV reads "Greeks" here.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV: "unto the Greeks")

why: "Greeks" repeats the word of 1:22 and is the easier reading, a scribe's matching. "Gentiles" is the harder, since "Jews and Gentiles" is the pair Paul uses elsewhere. The meaning is nearly the same.

t: "The things that are not" or "and the things that are not"
p: Some texts add "and" before the last group.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles
Westcott-Hort, Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV: "and things which are not")
readings.en: and the things that are not
readings.plain: and the things that are not

why: The word list shows "and" (kai) in Westcott-Hort, the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus, and not in SBL, NA28, Tyndale House or Tregelles. The sense is the same. The Plain follows the shorter form.

p: The Textus Receptus has "him" where the others have "God".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Byzantine majority text
Textus Receptus (KJV: "in his presence")

why: "God" is read by the Greek editions, including the Byzantine text. "Him" is found only in the Textus Receptus, and it reads as an easier, smoother line.

p: One Greek letter-group separates the two words.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles; Byzantine majority text, Textus Receptus (KJV: "the testimony of God")
NA28, Westcott-Hort

why: The Plain follows the SBL here. "Mystery" is attractive, because it matches the word at 2:7 and 4:1, but for that reason a scribe could have written it by habit. "Testimony" fits 1:6, "the testimony about Christ". The modern editions divide: NA28 and Westcott-Hort print "mystery"; SBL and Tyndale House print "testimony".
b: The two Greek words look alike (martyrion, mysterion). Either way Paul says he did not announce God's message with clever speech. If "mystery" is right, he is already naming the hidden plan he explains in 2:6-10.

t: "Persuasive wisdom", "persuasive words of wisdom" or "persuasive words of human wisdom"
p: Three forms of the phrase are printed. The KJV reads "enticing words of man's wisdom".

readings.w: SBLGNT (the only edition listed here that omits "words")
NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV: "enticing words of man's wisdom")

why: The word list shows "words" (logois) in NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text, and only the SBL text omits it. "Human" (anthropines) is found only in the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus, and may be a scribe's addition that matches the "human wisdom" of 2:13. The sense is the same in all three: Paul's message did not rest on clever persuasion. The Plain follows the SBL text and says it in the shortest way.
b: The SBL text reads a noun, peithoi ("persuasion"); the other forms read an adjective, peithois ("persuasive"), with "words". The two differ by a single letter, which is part of why editors disagree.

a: God revealed these things to us through the Spirit
p: The KJV reads "by his Spirit" and "But".

readings.w: SBLGNT: "for ... through the Spirit" (γάρ); NA28 and Tyndale House GNT: "but ... through the Spirit" (δέ)
readings.plain: God revealed these things to us through the Spirit

readings.w: Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV: "But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit")
readings.plain: God revealed these things to us through his Spirit

why: The editions without "his" are shorter, and "his" reads like a clarifying addition. There is also a small split between "for" (SBL) and "but" (NA28); the Plain leaves out the joining word and keeps the sense.

p: The Byzantine text adds "Holy".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV: "which the Holy Ghost teacheth")
readings.plain: words taught by the Holy Spirit

why: "Holy" is a common addition; the shorter reading is widely attested and Paul's usual way of saying it in this passage (2:10-14).

p: Two Greek words, sarkinos and sarkikos, look almost the same.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV: "carnal")

why: Sarkinos is the harder reading, since it is the rarer word, and sarkikos is the word of 3:3, which a scribe may have copied back. Strictly, -inos means "made of" and -ikos means "given to", but Paul may not keep the difference strictly, though some commentators think he does.
b: The same pair appears in Romans 7:14 in the site's Plain: "made of flesh" (sarkinos).

p: The KJV has a third item, "divisions".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine majority text, Textus Receptus (KJV: "envying, and strife, and divisions")

why: The shorter reading is the one in NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles; "dissensions" (dichostasiai) is added only in the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus. It matches the list in Galatians 5:20, which suggests a scribe added it.

p: The KJV reads "are ye not carnal?"

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV: "are ye not carnal?")

why: "Fleshly" repeats the word of 3:3 and so looks like a scribe's echo. "Merely human" is less expected and fits Paul's contrast between human and divine.

a: What then is Apollos? And what is Paul?
p: The KJV reads "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos?"

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: Τί οὖν ἐστιν Ἀπολλῶς; τί δέ ἐστιν Παῦλος;
readings.en: What then is Apollos? And what is Paul?
readings.plain: What then is Apollos? And what is Paul?

readings.w: Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV)
readings.orig: Τίς οὖν ἐστιν Παῦλος, τίς δὲ Ἀπολλώς, ἀλλ᾽ ἢ διάκονοι
readings.en: Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but servants
readings.plain: Who then is Paul? And who is Apollos?

why: The editions agree on "what" (the neuter), which asks about their role. The Byzantine text puts Paul first and uses "who", a smoother, more natural order. It is a case where the reading with Apollos first is the harder.

p: A small word, auto, is missing from the Byzantine text.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV: "the fire shall try")

why: The word list shows "itself" (auto) in NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles, and not in the Byzantine text or the Textus Receptus. The meaning is almost the same, with "itself" putting stress on the fire as the test.

p: The Byzantine text has a different pair of small words.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV: "Moreover it is required in stewards")
readings.en: and as for what is left

why: The word list shows "here" (hode) in the critical editions and "and what" (ho de) in the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus. The Plain follows the first and keeps "here", in the sense "in this matter". The KJV does not translate it. The meaning of the verse is not changed.

t: "Not beyond what is written" or "not to think beyond"
p: The Byzantine text adds a verb.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: the saying "Not beyond what is written"

readings.w: Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV: "not to think of men above that which is written")
readings.orig: τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ὃ γέγραπται φρονεῖν
readings.en: not to think beyond what is written
readings.plain: not to think beyond what is written

why: The shorter text has no verb and is more puzzling, so scribes probably added "to think" (phronein) to make a sentence. Some scholars have also suspected that the shorter text is itself damaged, and have proposed that the whole phrase was a marginal note.

p: The KJV reads "defamed", which renders the other reading.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Tregelles, Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV: "Being defamed")

why: Two near-synonyms: one for speaking ill of someone (dysphemeo), one for abusive speech (blasphemeo). The editions divide as the word list shows. The sense is the same.

p: Some texts leave out "Jesus".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort
Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus

why: The word list shows "Jesus" in SBL, NA28 and Westcott-Hort, and not in Tyndale House, Tregelles, the Byzantine text or the Textus Receptus. The sense is the same.
